agora.headline: Agora's Conversational AI Engine is a flat $0.10/agent-minute with no tiering by concurrency, region, model or stack — and the docs say explicitly "You are charged the same price even if you bring your own key (BYOK)." So a latency-vs-cost slider changes the Agora bill by exactly $0.00. The only thing that moves money is leaving the narrow Agora-managed-key list (ARES/Deepgram, OpenAI GPT-4o-mini/4.1-mini/5-nano/5-mini, MiniMax Turbo/OpenAI TTS-1) — at which point you pay $0.10 PLUS that vendor's own bill. The brief's premise is wrong on two vendors: Anthropic and ElevenLabs are NOT managed-key, so any stack using them is billed extra.

findings.claim: The Conversational AI Engine rate is a single flat $0.10 per agent-minute — no tier by concurrency, region, modality or model
findings.detail: Both the docs pricing page and the agora.io list-price page publish one line: 'Conversational AI Engine Audio Task | 0.10 | First 300 minutes are free'. There is no tier table, no region multiplier, no per-model rate, and no voice-vs-video split anywhere in the published rate card. Billing is monthly and aggregated across all projects under the developer account: free quota is subtracted from total usage, remainder multiplied by unit price, rounded to 2 dp. The only escape hatch published is 'If you have signed a sales contract with Agora, your billing follows the terms in your contract' and an 'Additional Discounts — Talk to Us' CTA.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/reference/pricing + agora.io/en/pricing/conversational-ai-engine/

findings.claim: DECISIVE FOR THE SLIDER: Agora charges the same $0.10 whether you use their managed key or bring your own — the fee is orchestration, not model pass-through
findings.detail: Verbatim footnote on both the docs and the commercial pricing page: 'The unit price includes usage of selected ASR, LLM, and TTS models. You are charged the same price even if you bring your own key (BYOK).' This means the $0.10 is a platform/orchestration fee that does not flex with model cost at all. Moving a slider from 'Lowest Cost' to 'Fastest' cannot change the Agora line item. The owner's instinct is correct and the wireframe's cost axis is currently modelling a price that does not exist.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/reference/pricing (footnote to unit price table)

findings.claim: The Agora-managed-key list is much narrower than the brief assumes — Anthropic and ElevenLabs are NOT included
findings.detail: The pricing page enumerates exactly what the managed key covers: ASR = ARES, Deepgram nova-2, Deepgram nova-3; LLM = OpenAI GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-5-mini; TTS = MiniMax 2.6 Turbo, MiniMax 2.8 Turbo, OpenAI TTS-1. The Supported vendors page corroborates with asterisks marking managed-key support: ARES*, Deepgram* (ASR); OpenAI* (LLM) only — Azure OpenAI, Cerebras, Claude Anthropic, Google Gemini, Google Vertex AI and Groq carry no asterisk; Minimax*, OpenAI* (TTS) only — Cartesia, ElevenLabs, Hume AI and Microsoft Azure carry no asterisk. So the brief's 'Agora resells OpenAI, Anthropic, Deepgram and ElevenLabs' is half right: OpenAI and Deepgram yes, Anthropic and ElevenLabs no.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/reference/pricing + docs.agora.io/en/conversational-ai/studio/build/supported-vendors

findings.claim: What ACTUALLY changes the bill is crossing off the managed-key list — that is a cliff, not a slope
findings.detail: Inside the managed list, every stack costs the same $0.10. Step outside it (Claude, Gemini, Groq, ElevenLabs, Cartesia, Hume, Azure, any MLLM) and you pay $0.10 to Agora PLUS that vendor's own bill, invoiced by the vendor to your own account — Agora never meters it. Note the structural consequence: no LLM stronger than GPT-5-mini and no premium TTS is on the managed list, so 'higher quality' stacks are inherently the ones that add a second bill. The real cost model is binary (included / included + vendor bill), which argues for a discrete state on the price badge rather than a continuous dollar figure.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/reference/pricing; supported-vendors; per-vendor docs (e.g. LemonSlice avatar requires your own api_key)

findings.claim: '$0.10/min, all in' is not accurate even for a fully managed stack — Audio RTC is billed on top
findings.detail: Agora's own worked example for a 10-minute all-managed session (ASR: ARES, LLM: GPT-4o-mini, TTS: MiniMax 2.8 Turbo) bills three lines: User A Audio RTC 10 min @ $0.00099 = $0.0099; Conversational AI Engine Audio Task 10 min @ $0.10 = $1.00; the ASR/LLM/TTS line @ $0.00 = $0.00. Total $1.0099. RTC is charged per participant-minute ($0.99 per 1000 participant minutes), so a multi-party channel scales that line. Small in absolute terms, but the wireframe's 'all in' claim is literally false and the third line at $0.00 is the honest way to show that models are included.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/reference/pricing (Examples section)

findings.claim: The wireframe's '750 ms' is not reachable under Agora's own published latency budget
findings.detail: Agora publishes end-to-end latency as RTC + algorithm preprocessing + ASR + LLM + TTS (+ avatar), with typical ranges: RTC 150-300 ms, algorithm preprocessing 720-940 ms, ASR time-to-last-word 400-700 ms, LLM TTFB/TTFS 250-1000 ms, TTS TTFB 100-350 ms, avatar 50-200 ms. Summing the minimums gives ~1620 ms. Separately, Agora's own benchmark leaderboard reports a best chained-model latency of 767.45 ms (Azure STT + Groq Llama 3.3 70B + Rime Mist) — but that figure excludes RTC and preprocessing. So 750 ms is roughly the chained-model best case for a non-managed stack, presented as if it were end-to-end for a managed one.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/best-practices/optimize-latency (verified raw markdown table)

findings.claim: The single biggest latency lever is a VAD setting, not the model bundle
findings.detail: The 720-940 ms preprocessing figure carries the footnote: 'Algorithm preprocessing latency is based on silence_duration_ms set to 640 ms. Adjusting this parameter affects preprocessing latency.' That one tunable is larger than the entire spread between the fastest and slowest managed LLM. Agora also states 'LLM typically contributes the most to overall latency' among the model components and recommends smaller models (gpt-4o-mini, gemini-2.5-flash), lower max_tokens, and stream: true so the agent starts speaking sooner. A slider that only swaps vendor bundles is moving the second-largest lever while hiding the largest.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/best-practices/optimize-latency

findings.claim: Agora exposes real per-turn latency telemetry, so a speed badge can be measured rather than asserted
findings.detail: The '111 agent metrics' webhook event emits per-turn asr_ttlw, llm_ttfb, llm_ttfs and tts_ttfb. Agora's published real-world sample shows turn 2 at asr_ttlw 141 / llm_ttfb 270 / llm_ttfs 482 / tts_ttfb 90, and turn 3 at asr_ttlw 103 / llm_ttfb 306 / llm_ttfs 948 / tts_ttfb 106 — note llm_ttfs nearly doubling between two turns of the same conversation. Latency is a distribution, not a constant, which is an argument for a badge showing a measured band from the user's own agent rather than a single hard-coded millisecond number.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/best-practices/optimize-latency (Real-world latency example)

findings.claim: Region selection has zero price effect but real quality and failover consequences — and the builder's region list matches Agora's geofence API exactly
findings.detail: properties.geofence.area accepts GLOBAL, NORTH_AMERICA, EUROPE, ASIA, INDIA, JAPAN, with an optional exclude_area when area is GLOBAL — a one-to-one match with the builder's control (Automatic = geofence disabled). No regional price variation is published anywhere. What does change: with geofencing off, Agora auto-deploys to the region matching the LLM URL's IP, falls back to the nearest available region, and fails over automatically. With it on, 'the system strictly limits access to the specified region and does not perform cross-regional failover', and a user outside the pinned region gets 'quality may be significantly impacted', with a hard error if all servers in that region are unavailable. The region control is a compliance-and-resilience trade, not a cost trade.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/best-practices/regional-restrictions

findings.claim: Conversational AI's 300 free minutes are separate from Agora's general 10,000 free minutes/month — the general bucket explicitly excludes it
findings.detail: The billing-policies free-of-charge section lists the ordered deduction sequence for the 10,000 monthly free minutes (broadcast streaming, voice/video/ILS, recording, cloud proxy, across HD/Full HD/2K tiers) and then carves out: 'Conversational AI Engine has its own free minutes policy.' The same callout excludes Signaling, Chat and IoT SDKs. Unused general free minutes are cleared at the end of each calendar month. A separate callout notes accounts on Agora's newer pricing model get 'a monthly free usage package by default instead of the 10,000 free minutes'.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/introduction/billing/billing-policies

findings.claim: No card is needed to start, but exceeding the free quota suspends a free account within a day — the card requirement is triggered by overage, not signup
findings.detail: An account is 'free' until you add a credit card, top up via bank, make a recent payment, or sign a contract. Agora suspends a free account 'on the second day after' either total usage exceeds the free quota of a service, or you use a product not included in the free quota — and during suspension no project can access Agora services. Adding a card unfreezes and upgrades to paid. On paid accounts, settlement runs on the 7th/14th/21st/28th: if available balance is in arrears by more than $50, auto-recharge fires if a card is linked; otherwise there is a 24-hour grace period before suspension. Separately, paid accounts are billed on the 1st for the prior month with automatic deduction on the 6th, and 5 days of negative balance after that triggers suspension.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/introduction/billing/billing-policies + docs.agora.io/en/introduction/billing/account-settlement

findings.claim: Avatar / video adds vendor cost with no published Agora rate — the rate card is audio-only
findings.detail: The published usage type is literally named 'Conversational AI Engine Audio Task'. No video or avatar per-minute Conversational AI rate is published. All avatar vendors (Akool, Anam, LiveAvatar/HeyGen, LemonSlice, Generic) are documented as requiring your own API key — e.g. LemonSlice takes api_key '<LEMONSLICE_API_KEY>' from your LemonSlice account — so avatar usage is billed by the vendor directly. Avatar also adds 50-200 ms of rendering latency. If the builder ever offers avatars, that is a second place where cost genuinely changes.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/reference/pricing; docs.agora.io/en/ai/models/avatar/lemonslice; llms/ai.txt avatar index

findings.claim: MLLM / realtime-model stacks have no managed-key option at all
findings.detail: The Supported vendors page lists MLLM vendors as Google Gemini Live, OpenAI Realtime API, OpenAI GPT-Live and xAI Grok — none carry the managed-key asterisk, and the customize-agent guide states 'No MLLM vendor-models are currently available under Agora Managed Key', requiring your own credentials. MLLM also collapses the latency chain (RTC + preprocessing + MLLM, no separate ASR/LLM/TTS), so it is the one architectural choice that genuinely changes both speed and cost — and it always adds a vendor bill.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/conversational-ai/studio/build/supported-vendors + customize-agent

findings.claim: A single agent session is capped at 72 hours regardless of idle timeout
findings.detail: The join API documents properties.idle_timeout with a valid range of 0 to 259200 seconds (72 hours), and adds: 'Regardless of the idle_timeout value, the maximum running time for a single session is 72 hours. The agent automatically exits after 72 hours.' Since billing runs from the moment the engine instance joins a channel until it exits, idle_timeout is a direct cost control — an agent left in an empty channel is still accruing $0.10/min. This is a more material cost lever than the model bundle.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/api-reference/api-ref/conversational-ai/join

findings.claim: Language coverage is a genuine axis that differs across stacks and is invisible in a cost/speed slider
findings.detail: Deepgram is documented as supporting real-time streaming ASR 'across multiple languages' with a per-agent language parameter (and keyterm boosting) that works in managed mode. MiniMax TTS is externally characterised as particularly strong on Chinese. Because the managed list is only ARES/Deepgram + OpenAI + MiniMax/OpenAI TTS, a customer needing a language or voice outside that set is forced into BYOK — meaning language need, not speed or thrift, is often the actual reason a bill changes. Agora does not publish a consolidated per-model language matrix.
findings.source: docs.agora.io/en/ai/models/asr/deepgram (managed mode + language/keyterm params)

findings.claim: The volume-discount table on the pricing page belongs to RTC, not to Conversational AI
findings.detail: agora.io/en/pricing/conversational-ai-engine/ renders a shared pricing shell: the Cloud Proxy rates ($0.99 / $3.99 / $8.99 per 1000 participant minutes), the PCU-based minimum monthly base fee tiers (Tier 1 ≤200 PCU = $500, Tier 2 201-1,000 = $1,000, Tier 3 1,001-2,000 = $2,000, Tier 4 2,001+ = contact sales) and the volume discount table (0-10K free, 100K-500K 5%, 500K-1M 7%, 1M-3M 10%) all sit in RTC/Cloud Proxy sections on that page. The Conversational AI block itself carries only the $0.10 list price and an 'Additional Discounts — Talk to Us'. Do not attribute those tiers to Conversational AI without confirming with Agora sales.
findings.source: agora.io/en/pricing/conversational-ai-engine/ (page structure)

findings.claim: Design implication: the two badges the owner wants are honest only if they measure different things — speed in milliseconds, price as a binary included/extra state
findings.detail: Given a flat $0.10, a price badge showing dollars will read identically at every slider position, which is exactly the incoherence the owner spotted. The defensible split is: SPEED badge = a measured latency band from the user's own agent (asr_ttlw + llm_ttfb + tts_ttfb from the 111 metrics event), shown as a range because Agora's own sample varies ~2x turn to turn; PRICE badge = 'Included in $0.10' vs 'Adds <vendor> billing' — a state, not a number, because that is genuinely what changes. The slider itself would be more truthful relabelled away from 'Lowest Cost — Fastest' (a false cost axis) toward something like 'Fastest — Highest quality', since within the managed set the real trade is latency against model capability, with cost constant until you leave the set.
findings.source: Synthesis of the Agora pricing footnote, supported-vendors asterisks, and the optimize-latency metrics

gaps: Whether the 300 free Conversational AI minutes are MONTHLY or ONE-TIME is genuinely ambiguous. The docs say 'At the end of each month, the free quota is subtracted from your total usage', which reads monthly; the pricing table just says 'First 300 minutes are free', which reads one-time, and several third-party summaries call it a one-time allocation. Agora does not state it unambiguously. Do not assert either reading in the UI without confirming with Agora.

No concurrency or PCU limit is published for the Conversational AI Engine. The PCU-based minimum monthly base fee tiers ($500/$1,000/$2,000) on the pricing page sit in the RTC/Cloud Proxy section. Whether a Conversational AI customer is subject to a PCU minimum, or to any cap on simultaneous agents, is unpublished — ask sales.

Volume discounts for Conversational AI are not published. The visible discount table (0-10K free, 100K-500K 5%, 500K-1M 7%, 1M-3M 10%) is in the RTC portion of the shared pricing page; the Conversational AI block offers only 'Additional Discounts — Talk to Us'. Treat any Convo AI volume tier as unknown.

No published per-minute rate for video or avatar Conversational AI. The rate card covers only the 'Audio Task'. Avatar vendors all require your own key, so avatar cost is vendor-side and unquantified by Agora.

Agora does not disclose what it pays its managed vendors, nor any per-model cost breakdown inside the $0.10. So there is no published basis for ever showing a different dollar figure per managed stack — any such number in the prototype would be invented.

No consolidated language-coverage matrix per managed model is published. Deepgram's language parameter is documented, but there is no Agora-published table of which languages each managed ASR/TTS supports — which matters because language need is a common reason to leave the managed set.

Whether the managed-key vendor list expands over time is unstated; it changed recently enough (GPT-5-nano/mini, MiniMax 2.8) that any hard-coded list in the builder will drift. The pricing page was last updated 2026-07-31 and supported-vendors 2026-09-11.

The live Performance Lab leaderboard did not render through WebFetch (the page is JS-driven), so the benchmark figures cited come from Agora's own Medium writeup rather than the live board. Per-stack numbers there are point-in-time and should be re-pulled from the live lab before being printed in a UI.

Not researched in this sweep: the EU/regional AI-disclosure legal grounding for the 'Tell the caller it's an AI' switch. Agora's geofence docs cover server residency only and say nothing about disclosure law. That question needs a separate legal-source sweep (EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations, US state bot-disclosure statutes, etc.) and should not be answered from Agora's docs.

market.headline: The slider's geometry is wrong before the badges are: across every platform that publishes per-model data, cheapest and fastest are the SAME end, not opposite ends — capability is the axis, and speed plus cost are both its consequences. Nobody in this market ships a slider; the best of them (Vapi) ships four named presets on a 2D space and prints three metrics per component, and ElevenLabs already ships exactly the two badges the owner is asking for (~797ms / ~$0.0082/min). At a genuinely flat $0.10 all-in, Agora is in Bland's position — and Bland, the one true flat-rate vendor, correspondingly exposes no model choice at all.

findings.claim: Cost and speed are correlated, not opposed — which makes the current "Lowest Cost — Balanced — Fastest" axis factually backwards
findings.detail: ElevenLabs' own LLM picker data (screenshotted in their help centre) ranks: Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite ~495ms / ~$0.0008/min (fastest AND cheapest), Claude 3 Haiku ~786ms / ~$0.0020, Claude Haiku 4.5 ~797ms / ~$0.0082, Claude 3.7 Sonnet ~1.09s / ~$0.0246, Claude Sonnet 4.5 ~1.69s / ~$0.0246, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview ~3.91s / ~$0.0170. The small models are simultaneously the quickest and the cheapest. Vapi states the mechanism outright: "More capable models usually respond more slowly... More capable models tend to be larger and take longer to begin generating a response" and High Intelligence "respond a little slower and cost more per minute than Balanced." Agora's slider puts Lowest Cost and Fastest at opposite poles, asserting that saving money costs you speed. The market data says saving money usually BUYS you speed, and what you actually give up is reasoning capability.
findings.source: ElevenLabs help centre screenshot + Vapi docs (presets, understanding-latency)

findings.claim: Vapi — the most developed example — deliberately refuses a single slider and uses four presets, because Cost Saver and Ultra Fast are different corners
findings.detail: Model Presets are "curated configurations that bundle a transcriber, model, and voice tuned for one goal": Balanced ("A strong all-round mix of quality, speed, and cost", the default for new assistants), High Intelligence ("Reasoning and conversation quality"), Ultra Fast ("Lowest latency"), Cost Saver ("Lowest cost per minute"). Vapi explicitly denies a monotonic axis: "Neither preset is always better than the other; choose based on whether your use case needs faster responses or stronger reasoning." Changing any single component moves the assistant to a fifth state labelled "Customized", and the displayed totals update. Four named goals on a 2D space — not one line.
findings.source: Vapi docs, Model Presets

findings.claim: ElevenLabs has already shipped the exact two-badge pattern the owner described — and the screenshot is public
findings.detail: In "Select primary LLM", every model row carries two right-aligned muted badges: a latency badge and a price badge, both prefixed with a tilde. Verbatim rows: "Claude Haiku 4.5   ~797ms  ~$0.0082/min", "Claude Sonnet 4.5   ~1.69s  ~$0.0246/min", "Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite   ~495ms  ~$0.0008/min". Units switch between ms and s at the 1-second boundary. Models are grouped by provider (Anthropic, Google, OpenAI) with "New" pills on recent releases, a "Search LLM" field at top, and a "Detailed costs" button pinned to the bottom of the sheet. Docs: "you can access estimated costs for each agent, based on its past behaviour and knowledge base, from the Detailed costs button in the Primary LLM selector in your agents settings." Note the tilde — every number is hedged as an approximation, and the price carries four decimal places because the LLM line is genuinely that small.
findings.source: ElevenLabs help centre, "How much does ElevenAgents cost?" (screenshot downloaded and read)

findings.claim: Vapi's "quality" is not one score — it is three different metrics chosen per component type, each from a named third-party benchmark
findings.detail: Transcriber quality = Word Error Rate, "the percentage of words the transcriber gets wrong", sourced from Daily's third-party STT benchmark, lower is better, "A WER of 5% means about 1 in 20 words is transcribed incorrectly." Model quality = "Intelligence", from the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 0–100, with a crucial caveat: "Voice agents run LLMs with reasoning turned off to keep latency low. The displayed scores reflect reasoning-off performance. The smartest voice agents run at around 20-30 intelligence score, be sure to compare models to each other for a relative benchmark." Voice quality = "Humanness", from the first-party Vapi Humanness Index, 1–100 via blind listening test. Vapi refreshes all metrics weekly and says so. This is the anti-pattern-avoidance move: they never invent a single composite "quality score".
findings.source: Vapi docs, Performance metrics and methodology reference

findings.claim: Vapi publishes the measurement boundary of its latency number and admits what it leaves out — this is the honesty bar to clear
findings.detail: "The displayed total adds the median latency for the transcriber, model, and voice." Components: transcriber = time to convert speech to text; model = time to first token; voice = time to first audio. Medians come from production calls, not lab conditions: "half of calls are faster and half are slower." And the admission: "The displayed total excludes endpointing and transport time. Both contribute to the delay a caller experiences. Endpointing can account for a meaningful share of that delay." Plus a warning against cross-vendor comparison: "Other latency figures may use ideal lab conditions or measure only one component... Compare figures only when their scope and conditions match."
findings.source: Vapi docs, understanding-latency and metrics-methodology

findings.claim: The gap between vendor latency claims and independently measured caller experience is roughly 2–3x — so the wireframe's bare "750 ms" is the riskiest number on the screen
findings.detail: Vendor claims: Vapi targets p50 below 500ms / p95 below 800ms; Retell "as low as about 600 ms"; Bland a "400 ms homepage figure" with "public methodology not stated"; Telnyx "sub-second" against a "450 ms architecture budget"; Twilio "491 ms p50, 713 ms p95" from an internal ConversationRelay test with "scope not fully disclosed"; ElevenLabs "about 75 ms" which is Flash TTS synthesis only and explicitly excludes endpointing, transcription, LLM inference, telephony and network. An independent 2026 benchmark measuring TTFAB (time to first audio byte) off the call's own audio — "from the moment the caller stops speaking to the moment the agent's audio starts", including endpointing, ASR, model turn, synthesis, network and telephony, 2,078 usable turns across 5 platforms — found medians of Telnyx 1,296ms, ElevenLabs 1,424ms, Bland 1,520ms, Vapi 1,558ms, Retell 1,740ms. A "750 ms" with no stated boundary is unfalsifiable and will not survive a customer measuring their own calls.
findings.source: Telnyx latency comparison (vendor-authored compilation) + Openbenchmarks independent TTFAB benchmark

findings.claim: Pricing SHAPE: six of nine are platform-fee-plus-pass-through, two are all-in bundles, one is all-in with no model choice at all
findings.detail: PASS-THROUGH: Vapi $0.05/min platform, "Models pass-through at cost" (Deepgram $0.0095–0.0099/min, OpenAI $0.0077–0.0452/min, ElevenLabs $0.0146–0.0238/min). Retell $0.055/min infrastructure + TTS $0.015–0.040/min + LLM $0.036–$0.32/min + telephony ~$0.015/min + per-feature add-ons (knowledge base +$0.005, denoising +$0.005, guardrails +$0.005, PII removal +$0.01, QA $0.10/min). ElevenLabs $0.08/min standard with LLM "billed separately on top, based on usage." LiveKit agent-session minutes ($0.01/min past plan allowance) plus separately-priced Inference per model. Telnyx $0.05/min and Twilio ConversationRelay $0.07/min, both with LLM and telephony on top. ALL-IN BUNDLE: Deepgram Voice Agent API, Standard $0.075/min covering STT+LLM+TTS, Advanced $0.163/min, with BYO discounts (BYO TTS $0.065, BYO LLM $0.059, BYO LLM+TTS $0.050). FLAT, NO MODEL CHOICE: Bland $0.14/min (Start) or $0.12/min (Build) — "Bland's per-minute rate covers the LLM, STT, and TTS in one number, with no token charges and no model-provider pass-throughs." Synthflow has withdrawn from published per-minute pricing entirely: enterprise contracts from $30,000 annually.
findings.source: Vendor pricing pages: vapi.ai/pricing, retellai.com/pricing, elevenlabs.io/pricing/agents, livekit.com/pricing, deepgram.com/pricing, bland.ai/pricing, telnyx.com/pricing/voice-ai-agents, twilio.com

findings.claim: Bland is the precedent that answers the owner's question directly: the one vendor with a genuinely flat all-in rate exposes no speed/cost control whatsoever
findings.detail: Bland charges $0.12–$0.14/min covering LLM, real-time transcription and premium voices in a single number, explicitly "no token charges and no model-provider pass-throughs", with only telephony and transfer minutes separate. Correspondingly there is no model picker, no preset row, no latency-versus-cost control in the product — because with an invariant rate there is nothing for such a control to report. This is the honest pairing. If Agora's $0.10 is truly flat across every stack, a price badge that changes with the slider would be fiction, and a price badge that never changes is not a badge — it is a reassurance, and belongs next to the Agora Managed Key, not on the slider.
findings.source: Bland AI pricing page and FAQ

findings.claim: Retell is the one vendor that sells latency directly as a line item — a "Fast Tier" priced at a multiple of the standard model rate
findings.detail: The pricing table has two columns, "Standard" and "Fast Tier", with Fast Tier at exactly 2x for most models: GPT 5.5 $0.16 → $0.32/min, GPT 5.4 $0.080 → $0.16, GPT 5.2 $0.056 → $0.112, GPT 5.1 $0.04 → $0.08, GPT 5.4 mini $0.036 → $0.072; GPT 4.1 is the exception at 1.5x ($0.045 → $0.0675), and Claude 5 Sonnet has no Fast Tier at all. Docs label it "Fast Tier (Premium Performance)" and describe it as routing "your LLM calls through dedicated, high-priority infrastructure for superior performance and consistency", quoting "50% reduction in latency variance", "25% improvement in average response time", "99.9% availability vs 99.5% standard". Note what is actually sold: not lower median latency so much as lower VARIANCE. That is a more honest thing to charge for, and a candidate second badge — p95, not median.
findings.source: Retell AI pricing page (scraped) and docs.retellai.com LLM options

findings.claim: Where the metrics are placed matters as much as what they say: Vapi puts them on the component panels AND inside every dropdown row, so the number is at the point of decision
findings.detail: "Performance metrics show latency, cost, and quality data for every transcriber, model, and voice. The data appears on component panels and the dropdown menu for each component." Choosing a preset updates everything downstream: "The transcriber, model, voice, and displayed totals update to match the preset." A third-party review of the builder describes a running readout at the top of the assistant screen — "a breakdown of cost and latency that changes as we experiment with different models" — reporting GPT-4o realtime preview at "$0.22 per minute with a latency of 700 ms" and o1-preview spiking to "8000 ms (8 seconds)", and notes Vapi "highlights the fastest and cheapest model by each provider" as tags. So: badges on each option, a live total for the whole stack, and superlative tags marking the extremes.
findings.source: Vapi docs overview/presets + Softailed Vapi review

findings.claim: Vapi publishes its cost-estimate assumptions in full — which is what makes a per-minute badge defensible rather than a guess
findings.detail: Transcriber is billed per audio minute and "Vapi transcribes audio from both the caller and the assistant. The estimate therefore includes two audio channels." Voice is billed per character "spoken in a typical minute". LLM = (input tokens per minute × effective input rate) + (output tokens per minute × output rate), where Vapi "estimates 5 requests per turn", "estimates 150 output tokens per minute based on typical generated speech in production call data", and blends standard and cached input rates "based on an assumed 50% cache hit rate". They publish the two ways the estimate is wrong: large cached prompts make actual cost lower, long calls make it higher because "growing conversation history is sent again with each request". And the disclaimer sits right on the number: "estimates for comparison rather than exact quotes... Use them to compare models consistently."
findings.source: Vapi docs, How voice agent component costs and estimates work

findings.claim: LiveKit sets the rigour standard for a latency number and it is far stricter than any badge: percentiles, named metric, published test conditions
findings.detail: Public dashboard reports per model TTFT (time to first token), TTFS (time to first sentence), total response time — each at p50/p95/p99 in ms — plus stream throughput at p50/p5/p1 tokens/sec. Conditions are stated: "~3,500-token system prompt with policies, FAQs and examples", a "nine-message support call", "5 tool definitions", "byte-identical requests... (128 max tokens, temperature 0.7, top-p 1.0)", re-run "Every 10 minutes, from a single vantage point". Sample results: Gemma 4 31B 313/956ms TTFT and 322/1,011ms TTFS; Gemini 2.5 Flash 534/1,110ms TTFT; GPT-4.1 567/1,557ms TTFT, 728/1,721ms TTFS. LiveKit's position is that TTFS is what the caller feels: "how long after the user stops talking before the agent starts speaking." Their production guidance targets P90 end-to-end under 3.5s and P99 under 5s — an order of magnitude looser than any marketing number, because it includes everything.
findings.source: LiveKit LLM Latency Benchmarks

findings.claim: Nobody calls the axis "speed vs cost" — the vocabulary is goal-named presets, and the three words in play are quality, speed and cost
findings.detail: Vapi's own summary line for Balanced is "A strong all-round mix of quality, speed, and cost" — three dimensions, and the preset names are goals not positions ("High Intelligence", "Ultra Fast", "Cost Saver"). Vapi's model metric is called "Intelligence", its voice metric "Humanness", its transcriber metric "Word error rate". Retell calls its upgrade "Fast Tier (Premium Performance)". Deepgram uses plain tier names, "Standard" and "Advanced". No vendor surveyed ships a literal slider for this trade-off, and no vendor labels an axis "speed vs cost". The naming convention is: name the goal, then print the evidence beside it.
findings.source: Vapi, Retell and Deepgram product and docs naming

findings.claim: How much the model choice actually moves the bill varies by two orders of magnitude between platforms — and this is the number that decides whether a price badge deserves to exist
findings.detail: On ElevenLabs the LLM line spans ~$0.0008 to ~$0.0246/min against a $0.08/min platform fee: the entire model choice moves the total by at most ~30%, and at the cheap end by under 1%. On Retell the LLM line spans $0.036 to $0.32/min against a $0.055/min infrastructure fee: the model choice can be six times the platform fee and utterly dominates the bill. On Deepgram the bundle itself steps from $0.075 to $0.163/min — a 2.2x jump between Standard and Advanced. On Bland it moves by exactly zero. A price badge earns its place in proportion to that spread; at Agora's flat $0.10 the spread is zero, which is precisely why the second badge has to be something other than price.
findings.source: Cross-reading of ElevenLabs, Retell, Deepgram and Bland pricing pages

findings.claim: Telnyx shows the failure mode of an "all-in" claim that isn't — worth avoiding given Agora is about to print "$0.10/min, all in"
findings.detail: The page headline is "$0.05 per minute. No fine print.", and the rate genuinely covers "Orchestration, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech in one rate." But LLM tokens are extra (~$0.004/min on Telnyx-owned GPUs, or pass-through for frontier models) and telephony is extra ("Starting at $0.0032/min"). Telnyx then concedes in its own copy that "A production agent lands near $0.056 per minute" — so the advertised all-in number is not the number anyone pays. If Agora prints "$0.10/min, all in", the line has to be true for the default managed-key agent including telephony, or it invites exactly this critique.
findings.source: Telnyx AI Voice Agent pricing page

findings.claim: The concrete recommendation the evidence supports for Agora's control
findings.detail: Replace the 1D slider with 3–4 named presets, because the trade is 2D and Vapi says so explicitly. Keep the owner's two badges but re-point them: badge one = SPEED, a latency figure with its boundary named in the label or tooltip, ideally p95 rather than median since Retell's data shows variance is what teams actually buy down; badge two = CAPABILITY, not price — Vapi's precedent is a third-party-sourced 0–100 Intelligence score with the reasoning-off caveat stated, which is defensible in a way an invented "quality score" is not. Then move price off the slider entirely and state it once, prominently, as the thing that does NOT change: "$0.10/min on every preset — Agora Managed Key, no vendor bills." That converts the flat rate from a hole in the UI into the strongest claim on the page, and it is a claim no competitor here can make. Reintroduce a live price badge only on the path where price genuinely varies — when a user leaves the managed key for their own vendor account, or picks a vendor outside the managed bundle — at which point it must carry a tilde and a stated assumption set, as both Vapi and ElevenLabs do. Finally, retire the bare "750 ms": every latency number needs its boundary, and the independent TTFAB data says an unqualified sub-second claim will not hold up.
findings.source: Synthesis of Vapi Model Intelligence docs, ElevenLabs LLM selector, Retell Fast Tier and Bland flat-rate precedent

gaps: Could not see the Vapi Model Intelligence UI directly — the dashboard is login-gated and the docs pages carry no screenshots (I checked the rendered HTML of all five Model Intelligence pages for image assets; there are none). Everything about Vapi's visual treatment comes from doc prose plus one third-party review, so the exact badge shapes, units and placement are inferred, not seen. Worth a paid trial account if the owner wants a shot of it.

Vapi does not publish which specific transcriber/LLM/voice each preset selects, nor a per-preset latency or cost figure in the docs. The docs only say the "displayed totals update to match the preset" — so I can confirm a total is shown per preset but not what it reads.
Deepgram does not document what actually differs between the Standard ($0.075/min) and Advanced ($0.163/min) Voice Agent tiers. A 2.2x price step with no published differentiator.
Twilio's pricing page does not state whether the $0.07/min ConversationRelay rate includes STT and TTS, or whether the LLM is bring-your-own. Only that "Voice costs are calculated separately".

The cross-platform latency comparison table is Telnyx-authored — a competitor marketing their own number as fastest — so I have marked it medium confidence. The independent Openbenchmarks TTFAB study is the better source but I could not verify its methodology beyond its own published description, and 432 turns per platform is a modest sample.

No vendor publishes a per-preset PRICE as a single headline number the way Agora's wireframe does. Vapi shows component-level costs that sum; ElevenLabs shows a per-model LLM cost against a separate platform fee. Agora would be first to print one all-in per-minute figure per preset — which is an opportunity, but means there is no precedent to copy for how to caveat it.

Whether Agora's $0.10 is genuinely invariant across all four vendor bundles is an internal question I could not check, and the entire recommendation hinges on it. If premium voices (ElevenLabs) actually cost Agora more than Deepgram+Azure, the flat rate is a margin decision rather than a physical fact, and a price badge might legitimately vary at the top of the range.

This sweep did not touch the second question in the brief — region-specific AI-disclosure legal grounding for the EU/US/India hosting-region control. That needs its own pass over the EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations, US state bot-disclosure statutes (California B.O.T. Act, Utah AIPA), and India's IT rules.

law.headline: Only the EU and South Korea impose a flat, proactive "tell them it's an AI" duty on a voice agent; the US has no federal AI-disclosure rule but does have a mandatory telephony script (caller identity + callback number) plus all-party recording consent in 11 states — so the region picker should pre-load a different sentence per region, and the EU's duty falls on the *provider* (Agora), not the builder's customer.

findings.claim: EU: Article 50(1) of the AI Act requires the system to be DESIGNED so the person is told they are dealing with an AI, unless it is obvious from context.
findings.detail: Operative text: "Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use." A phone voice agent is squarely in scope — the Commission's own FAQ says the duty covers systems "designed for a genuine two-way exchange with people" where "the AI itself communicates with the person rather than through a human intermediary." Product sentence: "In the EU you must tell the caller they are speaking to an AI, from the start of the call, unless it is already obvious."
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 50(1) — European Commission AI Act Service Desk (official)

findings.claim: EU: Article 50(5) sets the timing and manner — clear, distinguishable, at the latest at the first interaction, and accessible.
findings.detail: "The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 shall be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure. The information shall conform to the applicable accessibility requirements." For a voice agent this means the disclosure belongs in the opening greeting, before the agent starts doing work — not buried later, not only in a privacy notice. It also has to be perceivable on an audio-only channel, which rules out relying on a screen banner.
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 50(5) — EU AI Act (artificialintelligenceact.eu rendering of the OJ text)

findings.claim: EU: Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026 and was NOT delayed by the Digital Omnibus — this is live law today.
findings.detail: Article 113 makes 2 August 2026 the general application date, and Article 50 sits in Chapter IV, so it took effect on schedule. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (in force 27 July 2026), pushed the high-risk deadlines to 2 December 2027 (Annex III standalone) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I embedded) but left Article 50 untouched. Do not let a customer assume "the AI Act got delayed" — the transparency half did not.
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 113 (AI Act Service Desk) and Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (EUR-Lex)

findings.claim: EU: no instrument prescribes the WORDING. Only the substance, the timing and the clarity are fixed.
findings.detail: The Commission's Article 50 FAQ confirms no specific wording, format or channel is mandated — only that the disclosure be "in a clear and distinguishable manner" and "understandable and perceivable by natural persons," given "from the start of the first interaction." So the builder's editable sentence is legitimate, but the editor should enforce the substance (that it is an AI system) rather than let a customer water it down to something like "powered by smart technology." Recommend a validity check on the sentence, not a locked string.
findings.source: European Commission, "Transparency obligations under Article 50 of the AI Act" (official FAQ)

findings.claim: EU: the Article 50(1) duty sits on the PROVIDER, not the deployer — which means Agora carries it, not the builder's customer, unless the customer rebrands the agent as its own.
findings.detail: Art. 50(1) says "Providers shall ensure that AI systems ... are designed and developed" so the person is informed. That is a design-time duty, and it is Agora that designs and ships the builder. The deployer-facing duties in Art. 50(4) are narrower (deep fakes, and AI text published to inform the public on matters of public interest) and would not normally bite a customer-service voice agent. Product consequence: Agora should ship the disclosure ON by default in EU regions and make turning it off require a deliberate act, because the legal exposure for the design is Agora's. A customer that puts the agent on the market under its own name and trademark can itself become the provider — so the switch should record who turned it off.
findings.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 50(1) and 50(4); European Commission Art. 50 FAQ

findings.claim: EU: there are two official interpretive documents to link out to from the help section — the Commission's Article 50 Guidelines (final, 20 July 2026) and the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content.
findings.detail: The Commission published final Guidelines on the Article 50 transparency obligations on 20 July 2026 (draft 8 May 2026, consultation closed 3 June 2026). Separately, the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content — aimed at Art. 50(2) marking and 50(4) labelling — was confirmed by the Commission and the AI Board as adequate for demonstrating compliance; around 190 organisations had signed by end of July 2026. These are the right outlinks for a "what does the EU require?" help panel — they are the Commission's own, non-binding but authoritative.
findings.source: European Commission, Shaping Europe's Digital Future — Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content

findings.claim: US federal: there is NO federal rule requiring an AI agent to say it is an AI. Say this plainly in the UI.
findings.detail: As of 2026 there is no comprehensive federal AI statute and no enacted federal preemption of state AI law. The December 11, 2025 executive order "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence" set up a preemption process but has preempted nothing, and it explicitly targets state laws "compelling disclosures" as potentially First-Amendment-problematic — so the federal direction of travel is against mandated AI disclosure, not toward it. The binding US obligations on a voice agent come from telephony law and from individual states.
findings.source: Baker Botts, US AI Law Update (January 2026); CDT 2026 State and Federal AI Legislation tracker

findings.claim: US telephony: the FCC ruled AI-generated voices are "artificial" under the TCPA — so an outbound AI call needs PRIOR EXPRESS CONSENT before it is placed. This is the rule that actually bites.
findings.detail: FCC 24-17, Declaratory Ruling, CG Docket No. 23-362, adopted 2 February 2024, released 8 February 2024: "we confirm that the TCPA's restrictions on the use of 'artificial or prerecorded voice' encompass current AI technologies that resemble human voices and/or generate call content using a prerecorded voice. Therefore, callers must obtain prior express consent from the called party before making a call that utilizes artificial or prerecorded voice simulated or generated through AI technology." It adds: "These requirements are applicable to any AI technology that initiates any outbound telephone call using an artificial or prerecorded voice to consumers." For the builder: outbound batch calling with an AI voice is a consent-gated feature, not a dial-list feature. Inbound calls the consumer places are not affected.
findings.source: FCC 24-17 Declaratory Ruling (primary PDF, paras. 5 and 9)

findings.claim: US telephony: because the AI voice is "artificial," 47 CFR 64.1200(b) already mandates a script — the caller's legal business name at the START, plus a callback number. The builder's default sentence does not satisfy it.
findings.detail: Verbatim from the eCFR: "All artificial or prerecorded voice telephone messages shall: (1) At the beginning of the message, state clearly the identity of the business, individual, or other entity that is responsible for initiating the call. If a business is responsible for initiating the call, the name under which the entity is registered to conduct business with the State Corporation Commission (or comparable regulatory authority) must be stated; (2) During or after the message, state clearly the telephone number ... of such business ..." plus (3) an automated opt-out mechanism within two seconds of the identification for telemarketing calls. This is a legal-name requirement, not a brand requirement. "You're talking to an AI assistant." is legally inert here — the mandatory US sentence is an IDENTITY sentence, and it is a separate field from the AI-disclosure sentence. The builder should model them as two fields, not one.
findings.source: 47 CFR § 64.1200(b) (eCFR, current)

findings.claim: California SB 1001 (the BOT Act) almost certainly does NOT reach a telephone voice agent — it is limited to "online" communication, and it only bites on intent to mislead for a sale or an election.
findings.detail: BPC § 17941(a) makes it unlawful "to use a bot to communicate or interact with another person in California online, with the intent to mislead the other person about its artificial identity for the purpose of knowingly deceiving the person about the content of the communication in order to incentivize a purchase or sale of goods or services in a commercial transaction or to influence a vote in an election." BPC § 17940 defines "online" as "appearing on any public-facing Internet Web site, Web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication." A PSTN call is not that. So: the BOT Act applies to a web-embedded chat or voice widget, not to a phone call — and even then only where there is intent to deceive tied to a sale or a vote. The safe harbour is in § 17941(b): "The disclosure required by this section shall be clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed to inform persons with whom the bot communicates or interacts that it is a bot." Operative since 1 July 2019.
findings.source: California Business and Professions Code §§ 17940–17942 (official leginfo)

findings.claim: California SB 243 (companion chatbots) has been in force since 1 January 2026 and carries a private right of action — but it targets companion/emotional chatbots, not customer-service voice agents.
findings.detail: SB 243 requires operators to disclose the chatbot's artificial nature where a reasonable person would be misled into thinking they are talking to a human, to notify minors repeatedly, to block sexually explicit content with minors, and to run suicide/self-harm protocols. It is the first CA chatbot law with a private right of action — injunctive relief, damages with a $1,000-per-violation floor, and fees. Scope note for the product: a scheduling or support agent is out of scope; a "companion"-style agent is in. Worth a scope warning in the builder rather than a blanket disclosure.
findings.source: California SB 243 (2025), effective 1 Jan 2026 — Future of Privacy Forum analysis of the enacted bill

findings.claim: Utah is the most product-relevant US state: disclosure is required ON REQUEST in any consumer transaction, and PROACTIVELY at the start of a verbal interaction in high-risk / regulated-occupation contexts.
findings.detail: Utah Code § 13-77-103 (effective 7 May 2025, as amended by SB 226): a supplier using generative AI to interact with an individual in connection with a consumer transaction must disclose that the individual is interacting with generative AI and not a human IF the individual asks or otherwise prompts — the ask must be a clear and unambiguous request to determine whether they are talking to a human or an AI. For regulated occupations (Department-of-Commerce-licensed: health, legal, financial and similar) the disclosure is proactive and must be given VERBALLY at the start of a verbal interaction. § 13-77-104 is a safe harbour: no enforcement action if the AI "clearly and conspicuously discloses at the outset ... and throughout the interaction that it is generative artificial intelligence, is not human, or is an artificial intelligence assistant." Two product consequences: (1) the agent must be able to answer "are you a real person?" truthfully — that is a prompt/behaviour requirement, not a greeting requirement, and the builder has no control for it today; (2) the Utah safe-harbour phrasing is the closest thing to a model sentence any US instrument offers.
findings.source: Utah Code Title 13, Chapter 77 §§ 13-77-103 and 13-77-104 (Utah Legislature); SB 226 (2025)

findings.claim: Colorado: SB 24-205 is dead — it was repealed and replaced by SB 26-189 (effective 1 January 2027), and the chatbot disclosure duty now lives in a separate law, HB 26-1263.
findings.detail: SB 24-205's blanket "disclose that the consumer is interacting with an AI system" was never enforced: its start slipped from 1 February 2026 to 30 June 2026, a federal court blocked enforcement, and Governor Polis signed SB 26-189 on 14 May 2026 replacing it, effective 1 January 2027. SB 26-189 is an automated-decision-making (ADMT) law about consequential decisions — employment, credit, housing, insurance — with advance notice and post-decision disclosure, not a conversational-AI rule. The chatbot rule moved to the Chatbot Safety Act, HB 26-1263, signed 1 July 2026, which requires operators of publicly accessible conversational AI services to "disclose prominently that users are interacting with AI, not a human," plus age estimation, minor protections, self-harm protocols and annual AG reporting. Colorado AG rulemaking on both was filed 11 August 2026 with comments open to 26 October 2026 — so the detail is still moving.
findings.source: Colorado General Assembly SB26-189; Colorado AG ADMT & Chatbot Safety rulemaking page

findings.claim: US call recording: 11 states require ALL-party consent, and this bites regardless of AI. It is a separate sentence from the AI disclosure and the builder has no control for it.
findings.detail: All-party ("two-party") consent states as of 2026: California, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Washington. Connecticut requires all-party consent for phone recordings specifically. Practically every AI voice agent records and transcribes, so a US-facing agent needs a recording notice in the opening — typically "this call may be recorded" — with continued participation treated as implied consent. This is the single most-likely-to-be-missed requirement in the builder: the "Tell the caller it's an AI" switch has no sibling for "Tell the caller it's recorded," and the recording notice is the one that is actually mandatory in California while the AI notice is not.
findings.source: Digital Media Law Project, Recording Phone Calls and Conversations (state-by-state); MWL 50-state recording chart

findings.claim: India: NO binding duty to tell a caller they are talking to an AI. The 2026 IT Rules bite on synthetic MEDIA and on platforms, not on live one-to-one voice agents.
findings.detail: MeitY notified the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026 via G.S.R. 120(E) on 10 February 2026, effective 20 February 2026. New Rule 2(1)(wa) defines "synthetically generated information" as audio/visual content "artificially or algorithmically created ... in a manner that such information appears to be real, authentic or true, and depicts or portrays any individual or event in a manner that is, or is likely to be perceived as indistinguishable from a natural person or a real-world event." New Rule 3(3) puts labelling, provenance-metadata and anti-tamper duties on INTERMEDIARIES that offer SGI tools — MeitY's FAQ names "voice synthesis / voice cloning tools" explicitly. For audio, the label must be "a prefixed audio disclosure" plus embedded permanent metadata. So: Agora, as a provider of voice synthesis, plausibly has Rule 3(3) duties in India; the builder's customer running a support line with a generic synthetic voice that impersonates nobody most likely does not meet the SGI threshold at all. Say plainly in the UI: India has no "declare you are an AI" rule for a live call.
findings.source: MeitY FAQs on the Amendment to the IT Rules on Synthetically Generated Information (official PDF), Q5, Q19, Q20

findings.claim: Japan: NO binding disclosure requirement. The AI Promotion Act has no penalties and no mandatory obligations — transparency is a "reasonable efforts" duty only.
findings.detail: The Act on Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies (2025, in full effect since late 2025) is a promotion statute: basic principles, an AI Basic Plan, ministry guidelines, information-gathering and requests for cooperation. It creates no prohibited uses, no penalties, and no compliance obligations. Transparency is framed as doryoku gimu — a non-binding best-efforts duty common in Japanese legislation. Product copy should say so without hedging: "Japan does not require this. The disclosure is recommended practice, not law." That honesty is worth more to the user than a vague "consult your counsel."
findings.source: Japanese Government, HIGHLIGHTING Japan (Nov 2025) and OECD.AI policy entry for the Act; White & Case analysis of the enacted law

findings.claim: Asia: South Korea is the one Asian jurisdiction with a binding, proactive, EU-style notification duty — Article 31 of the AI Framework Act, in force 22 January 2026.
findings.detail: Under Art. 31(1) an AI business operator offering high-impact or generative-AI-powered products or services must notify users IN ADVANCE that the product or service uses AI. Art. 31(2) requires indicating that generative output was generated by generative AI. Art. 31(3) covers content "difficult to distinguish from reality" — squarely a realistic synthetic voice — requiring notice or display that it was AI-generated. So a Korean-facing voice agent needs the disclosure up front, like the EU. If the builder's "Asia" region resolves to a Korean edge, the disclosure should default ON, not to "recommended."
findings.source: Framework Act on AI Development and Establishment of a Foundation for Trustworthiness (Korea), Art. 31 — Future of Privacy Forum and Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor

findings.claim: Asia: China requires labelling of AI-generated audio, but the duty is on service providers and the mechanism is labels plus metadata, not a spoken sentence.
findings.detail: The CAC's Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Synthetic Content, with mandatory national standard GB 45438-2025, took effect 1 September 2025. They require both explicit labels (visible/audible prompts) and implicit labels (metadata or watermarks in file headers) on generated text, image, AUDIO, video and virtual scenes, imposed on internet information service providers and content-distribution providers. For an audio stream this is closer to Agora's platform obligation than to a script the builder's customer writes. Flag rather than solve: China is not in the builder's region list, and a China-facing deployment raises licensing questions beyond disclosure.
findings.source: CAC Measures for Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content (translation) + GB 45438-2025

findings.claim: North America beyond the US: Canada has NO in-force AI disclosure law. AIDA died on 6 January 2025 and has no successor.
findings.detail: Bill C-27 and the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act inside it were extinguished when Parliament was prorogued on 6 January 2025, and as of mid-2026 no replacement bill has been introduced. What governs is PIPEDA, the voluntary ISED Code of Conduct for generative AI, and Quebec's Law 25 — whose s. 12.1 automated-decision duty is a right to be informed of, and seek human review of, decisions made exclusively by automated processing of personal data. That is a decision-notice rule, not a "you are talking to an AI" rule. If the builder's "North America" region spans Canada, the right copy is: no Canadian requirement; the US state and telephony rules are what drive the setting.
findings.source: Government of Canada Bill C-27 status (died on prorogation); Quebec Law 25 s. 12.1

findings.claim: What a compliant sentence must actually SAY: no instrument anywhere prescribes wording, but three different substances are required and the builder currently models only one.
findings.detail: Substance 1 — AI status: that the person is interacting with an AI system and not a human (EU Art. 50(1); Korea Art. 31; Utah safe harbour; CO HB 26-1263). No prescribed words. Utah's safe-harbour formula is the most defensible model text because it is the only one a legislature has written down: "generative artificial intelligence, is not human, or is an artificial intelligence assistant." Substance 2 — caller identity: the registered legal business name at the beginning of the call, plus a callback number (47 CFR 64.1200(b)) — mandatory on every US outbound AI-voice call, and completely absent from the builder. Substance 3 — recording notice: required in 11 all-party-consent US states and, in the EU, driven by GDPR lawful-basis and transparency rather than by the AI Act. Recommendation: split the single switch into three rows that share one preview of the actual opening line the caller will hear, and show the region's requirement as a per-row state (Required / Recommended / Not required) rather than one global toggle.
findings.source: Synthesis of 47 CFR 64.1200(b), Utah Code 13-77-104, EU AI Act Art. 50(1) and (5), Korea AI Framework Act Art. 31

findings.claim: Deployer vs provider, summarised for the product: Agora carries the EU design duty and probably India's Rule 3(3) tool duty; the customer carries every telephony duty.
findings.detail: EU Art. 50(1) — provider (Agora designs the builder, so Agora should ship the disclosure on by default in EU regions). EU Art. 50(4) — deployer, but only for deep fakes and public-interest text, so normally not engaged. India Rule 3(3) — intermediary offering the voice-synthesis tool, i.e. Agora, not the customer. TCPA consent, 64.1200(b) identity and callback, state recording consent, Utah's on-request answer, Colorado's chatbot disclosure — all sit on the party that initiates the call and runs the consumer transaction, i.e. the customer. This split is the argument for making the disclosure switch a defaults-and-warnings surface rather than a free toggle: Agora's own exposure is in the default, the customer's is in the override.
findings.source: Synthesis of Reg (EU) 2024/1689 Arts. 50(1)/50(4); India IT Rules 2021 (as amended 2026) Rule 3(3); 47 USC 227 and 47 CFR 64.1200

findings.claim: Coming, not yet law: the FCC has a pending rulemaking that WOULD require an AI disclosure at the start of every AI-voice call in the US.
findings.detail: FCC 24-84, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking adopted 7 August 2024 in the same CG Docket 23-362, proposes requiring callers to disclose AI-generated voice both when collecting consent and "at the beginning of each call, clearly disclose to the called party that the call is using AI-generated technology." Comments closed October 2024; no final rule has been adopted as of August 2026, and the current FCC's deregulatory posture plus the December 2025 preemption EO make the timing genuinely uncertain. Worth a "proposed, not in force" line in the help panel — it is the single change that would flip the US from Recommended to Required.
findings.source: FCC 24-84 NPRM, CG Docket No. 23-362 (proposed rules, not adopted)

rec.sliderVerdict: The owner is right, and the code proves it: at all three stops `stackCost()` returns `platformPerMin` $0.10 and `vendorPerMin` 0, so `stackEstimateFor().costPerMin` is $0.10 at "Lowest Cost" and $0.10 at "Fastest". The track-end line under the slider literally renders "1050 ms, ~$0.10/min" on the left and "660 ms, ~$0.10/min" on the right. The word "Cost" on that axis is measuring a number that never moves, because Agora's rate is a flat orchestration fee that the docs say is charged identically under BYOK. What the slider actually trades is latency against model capability: 1050 ms on Claude Haiku plus non-streaming Whisper, 660 ms on Deepgram Nova-3 plus GPT-4o-mini. There is a second, worse problem underneath it. `MANAGED_PROVIDERS` in campaign-data.ts lists Anthropic and ElevenLabs as resellable, and Agora's pricing page does not: the managed key covers only ARES and Deepgram for ASR, OpenAI mini and nano models for LLM, and MiniMax Turbo and OpenAI TTS-1 for TTS. Corrected against the real list, the "Lowest Cost" preset is the only stop where all three slots leave the managed set (Whisper, Claude, Azure), so it would bill $0.143/min against Balanced's $0.116 and Fastest's $0.14. The cheap end is the expensive end. So: rename the axis to Fastest / Balanced / Most capable, rebuild the three bundles from managed models only so every stop genuinely is $0.10, and let the price badge become a number only when a slot goes BYO, which is the one place the money is real.

caveats: The region control is where the AGENT RUNS, not where the CALLER is, and the law follows the caller. Ship this map as a prompt, not a determination. Exact copy for the row: "This is where your agent runs. What the law asks for depends on where your callers are. If they are somewhere else, use their rules." MANAGED_PROVIDERS at lib/campaign-data.ts:1740 is wrong and it is load-bearing, because it is what `slotMode` and the backup-provider logic read. It lists Anthropic at 0.029 and ElevenLabs at 0.046 as resellable. Managed status is per MODEL, not per vendor. OpenAI gpt-4o is not on the managed list; gpt-4o-mini is. A vendor-keyed `MANAGED_PROVIDERS` map cannot express that. Add a `managed: boolean` field to each STACK_CATALOG entry and have `stackCost` read it, which also makes the list auditable when Agora adds models (it changed recently enough to add GPT-5-nano and MiniMax 2.8).

All three current preset bundles leave the managed set on at least one slot, so under the corrected list none of them is actually $0.10. Do not print a measured-from-telemetry latency band yet. Agora's 111 agent metrics webhook emits per-turn asr_ttlw, llm_ttfb, llm_ttfs and tts_ttfb, and Agora's own published sample shows llm_ttfs going from 482 ms to 948 ms between two turns of one conversation. That is the right long-term source for the speed badge, and it makes the badge measurable instead of asserted, but it needs the agent to have run. The disclosure switch and the sentence field currently model one substance, and there are three. AI status (EU, Korea, Utah), caller identity (47 CFR 64.1200(b): registered legal business name plus callback number, mandatory on every US outbound AI call, entirely absent from the builder), and recording notice (11 all-party-consent states). Split the one switch into three rows sharing the existing "Callers hear" composed preview, and show the region's answer per row as Required / Recommended / Not required rather than as one global toggle.

EU Article 50(1) is a duty on the PROVIDER, which means it is Agora's exposure, not the customer's, unless the customer rebrands the agent as its own. EMPTY_DRAFT already ships `disclose: true` for new agents, which is the right call. Add a confirm step and an audit record on turning it off while the region is Europe or Asia, since the design decision is Agora's to defend.

Utah Code 13-77-103 and 13-77-104 could not be read from the primary source in the research sweep (le.utah.gov refused connections, Justia and FindLaw returned 403). The North America requirement sentence and the safe-harbour-derived default sentence are consistent across two independent search extracts, but verify the exact subsection text against le.utah.gov before shipping that copy.

An FCC rulemaking (FCC 24-84, CG Docket 23-362) proposes requiring an AI disclosure at the start of every US AI-voice call. It is proposed, not adopted. Worth one line in the North America help panel, because it is the single change that would flip that region from Recommended to Required.
